images.text:
An informational interview is a way to gain first-hand information about working in a certain industry. It is not a way of gaining employment, rather it is a networking strategy. An informational interview will give you a chance to have a discussion about the industry, the challenges associated with it, networking secrets, and other topics you may have wanted to know about.
You should complete informational interviews with people who are in jobs that you're interested in. They can be people you used to work with or individuals you've identified on your own. For example, if you're interested in teaching, you could talk to one of your professors, or a recent graduate who is now a teacher.

THE PROCESS
ARRANGE MEETINGS: Always be professional and polite in requesting an interview. People are busy, so it is appropriate to request a 30-minute meeting. The time will go very quickly, so be prepared with your questions.
BE A PROFESSIONAL: Make sure to bring a resume, note pad and a pen for your notes. Your style of dress can be more casual than a real interview, nevertheless you should look professional.

BE CONFIDENT: Start by introducing yourself and why you set up the interview. Then, mention that you have some questions that you would like to ask. The questions will dictate the flow of conversation.
FOLLOW THROUGH: After wrapping up the conversation, make sure to ask if there are any other people and/or organizations they can recommend for future informational interviews. If so, ask for their contact information and if you may use their name to connect with them.
EXHIBIT PROFESSIONAL ETIQUETTE: Do a follow-up. This can be by sending a thank you letter or email.

Networking is the practice of meeting other people involved in the same kind of work, to share information, support each other etc.  Before you start networking, you should assess your interests and skills and a field you want to investigate. Then, you identify potential professionals to contact. Here are some tips to help you:
<li>Contact the people you identified and ask if they are willing to answer a few of your questions via e-mail or partake in a telephone informational interview.
<li>If you are interested in a phone interview, clearly state the time at which you will call to arrange the interview and follow through with this plan in your e-mail.
<li>You can also ask the person to suggest a time by e-mail if they prefers and say you will call to arrange the interview if there is a time conflict, or if you don't hear from them.
<li>If you want to ask a few questions in an e-mail, ask if this is okay and wait for a response.  Remember, these professionals can be very busy with work.
<li>You may need to try more than once to contact them and they may not respond at all.
<li>Allow a minimum of one week between your initial contact and a second attempt.
